reasoning: The crash described in the finding is real, and nothing along the path stops it. (1) Source: the wire decoder takes any finite Double for utilization with no range check (AnthropicWireTypes.swift:71, via AppConfig.swift:199-203). UsageWindow.swift:20 stores it as-is, UsageSnapshot.swift:71 takes the max of the windows, and VendorViewModel.swift:274-276 appends that value to history. UsageHistoryStore.swift:56-58 writes it to JSONL. 1e300 encodes fine; only inf/NaN would fail. (2) Reload: VendorViewModel.swift:150-155 loads 24h of samples on every launch, and neither load() nor SparklineView.swift:24 (time filter only) checks the value. (3) Sink: SparklineView.swift:46 sets maxPercent to the largest sample. yFor at :58-60 clamps only the drawing coordinates. The label at :126 runs Int(maxPercent.rounded()) when maxPercent > current+5, and :116 runs Int(last.max.rounded()). In Swift, Int(Double) traps when the value is out of range, so the app hard-crashes when the expanded card renders. So the claimed damage holds: the popover crashes on every relaunch until the sample falls out of the 24h window, and the user has no in-app fix because the popover crashes before they can act. Impact is availability only: no data is disclosed or written beyond the one bad number. The attacker must control an HTTPS response from an allowlisted vendor host, which is a strong precondition. That makes the finding's LOW severity right, but the harm itself is real.
